lines.text: The Mountain Never Knew Its Name
When I was a boy, the atlas seemed permanent.
Every country had a colour. Every border had a line.
I didn’t know the ink was still wet.
The atlas of my childhood Is a book of vanished names;
The mountains never moved an inch— We only moved the frames.
We shouted over what to call them, As though the stone might care;
They wore no names before we came, And none when we’re not there.
Flags changed in the same old wind, New colours filled the page;
Yesterday’s familiar neighbour Became the foe of another age.
We taught our children lines were nations, As though ink ran through the ground;
Then wondered why they marched to die Whenever lines moved round.
But the mountain never knew its name, The river never chose a side;
Rulers drew their lines in ink, The people traced them out in lives.
They raised a flag, declared a victory, And toasted everything they’d gained;
While far above the graves below, The mountain never knew its name.
In guarded rooms, important boys Lean closely over maps;
Moving borders with a fingertip From safety behind glass.
They speak of blood and destiny, Of honour, soil and pride;
But never hear the first shell fall Or watch the children hide.
They dream of being carved in stone, Their names remembered when they’re gone;
And build their road to immortality With other people’s sons.
Five inches on the general’s map, A lifetime from the trench;
They moved his drinks cabinet forward And paid for it in flesh.
Men vanished there by thousands For mud they’d lose by dawn;
The dispatch called it progress— The widows carried on.
A station changed hands fourteen times
Before the day was done; Fourteen victories on paper—
And nobody had won.
They captured broken bricks and rails,
Then lost them in the smoke; Each general moved his pencil—
Another family broke.
Ask the ones who pay for glory What they actually desire:
A roof that keeps the winter out, Some food, some warmth, some fire.
A little left when bills are paid, Their children home at night;
A loaf that doesn’t cost their firstborn, And the freedom to live their lives.
They do not dream of empires. They do not hunger for a throne.
They only want a little peace And a place to call their own.
But when madness comes from common men, We lock it behind doors;
When madness rises from a palace, We dress it up as war.
Insanity wore medals And called the madness brave;
The powerful talked of history—
The powerless dug the graves.
Still the mountain never knew its name. The river never chose a side.
No field demanded ownership. No forest asked that people die.
The flags will fade, the maps will change,
The proudest empires fall; The land does not belong to us—
It only carries us all.
We came as guests and called ourselves kings,
Drew borders, conquered, killed and claimed; Then disappeared like summer rain—
And the mountain never knew our names.

She wakes up before the house does, before the kettle screams,
before the little feet come running through the wreckage of her dreams.
There’s lunches on the counter, there’s washing on the line,
there’s a body full of warning lights that still says, “Yeah, I’m fine.”
She counts the stairs like mountains, checks the floor like it’s the sea,
and laughs, “If I go down again, at least the carpet’s free.”
But there’s a switch behind her eyes she flips before the day begins,
puts a smile across the cracks and lets nobody in.
She’s holding up the sky with shaking hands and stubborn bones,
fighting wars in quiet rooms that nobody else knows.
And if the world starts spinning, she’ll joke, “Well, here we go,”
because standing is overrated when your heart says no.
She’s tired, but she’s trying, bent but never broken through,
and God help gravity when she’s got things to do.
Two kids need their mother, a boy, a girl, a thousand things,
school bags, tears and dinosaurs, lost shoes and fairy wings.
Her husband’s fighting shadows that sit heavy in the air,
so she becomes the lighthouse while forgetting she needs care.
At work she wears her armour, polished bright and paper-thin,
answers emails, joins the meetings, keeps the thunder locked within.
She’s mastered looking normal while her pulse is climbing walls,
smiling like a saint while internally she crawls.
She’s holding up the sky with shaking hands and stubborn bones,
fighting wars in quiet rooms that nobody else knows.
And if the world starts spinning, she’ll joke, “Well, here we go,”
because standing is overrated when your heart says no.
She’s tired, but she’s trying, bent but never broken through,
and God help gravity when she’s got things to do.
Some days she’s queen of the sofa, ruler of the floor,
negotiating peace talks with the handle of the door.
“Just one more minute,” she whispers, “then I’ll rise and face the mess.”
A warrior in compression socks, wearing chaos like a dress.
And no, she doesn’t want pity, no parade, no golden crown,
just someone who can see her when she has to sit back down.
She’s holding up the sky with shaking hands and stubborn bones,
loving through the hard days in a house that needs a home.
And if the world starts spinning, she’ll laugh through “not again,”
because dark jokes are cheaper than a breakdown now and then.
She’s tired, but she’s trying, braver than she’ll ever claim,
and even when she’s trembling, she is still a bloody flame.
So here’s to every morning she somehow makes it through,
to the woman behind “I’m fine,” who deserves an “I see you.”
And if today she can’t stand tall, let the whole world wait instead—
because heroes need the sofa too, and coffee, salt, and bread.

Ten years old beneath a southern sky, A quarter acre, a house, and room to breathe.
Then an ocean carried me to Europe, To walls of stone and unfamiliar streets.
Whole lives were stacked above each other, Floor upon floor and row on row.
Like rabbit hutches built for people— Or so it seemed, so long ago.
But every hilltop held a castle, Every old wall hid a tale;
Knights and kings and ancient battles, Church bells drifting through the vale.
The towns back home felt new and open; Here the centuries stood in stone.
Forests, fields and village pathways Slowly made me feel at home.
Then at sixteen, southern waters Called me back beneath their blue.
To the hills I still remembered, And the life I thought I knew.
I thought home was earth beneath me, A roof, a key, a piece of ground;
The country where my road had started, With fences running all around.
But a place can fill your senses, Be the finest you have known—
And still be only beautiful When you must stand there alone.
There I worked and there I married, Built my houses, laid my claim;
Collected all the proof of living— Doors and deeds beside my name.
Then she left, and every room grew colder
Than the empty years before. Ten years buried in the working,
Never asking any more. Working hard enough to feel nothing,
Just surviving, marking time; Living—but not feeling alive.
Then word arrived across the water: My father’s health was failing there.
I packed one year into a suitcase, Thinking time might still repair
All the distance left between us, All the words we’d never known.
It didn’t happen as I’d hoped it— But that road still led me home.
For there I found the one who saw me, Saw the man beneath the scars.
We fell in love and built a marriage, Then our daughter joined our hearts.
Now I know home isn’t country, It has no border, flag or throne.
New Zealand’s hills still live within me; Europe’s written in my bones.
I love the wild and open distance. I love the history carved in stone.
But either one without you Would be beautiful—and cold.
If I could, I’d chase the summer, Six months underneath each sky;
Walk among the ancient castles, Watch the southern clouds roll by.
But no landscape shares the silence. No horizon holds my hand.
Paradise is only scenery Without someone who understands.
And one day houses pass to strangers, Keys fall from our empty hands.
All the things we worked to gather Find another place to stand.
What remains are lives we’ve touched, Every kindness that we shared;
Every heart that carries something Of the time when we were there.
Let the road cross any ocean. Let me wander near or far.
Home was never where I started— Home is wherever you are.

lines.text: Mind the gap.
Mind the bike. Mind the—
Never mind.
I sat alone in a café, Just coffee in my hand;
No phone, no screen, no laptop— The last unconnected man.
Around me, heads were bowed down To little gods of glass;
I watched the whole world passing— They just watched the adverts pass.
On buses and on railways, It’s the same wherever you go:
Fifty faces lit by screens— And one old fool watching the show.
I shake my head— But just inside;
Apparently I’m the weird one For looking up outside.
Look up! Look out! Life is happening now!
You can Google where you are If you live to work it out.

lines.text: We walk where ancient branches meet, Where broken sunlight finds our feet,
Through scattered leaves and fallen wood, And everything is still... and good.
The old oaks whisper overhead, A thousand shades of green are spread,
The wind moves softly through the trees, And carries summer on the breeze.
Behind me voices rise and fall, Soft conversation through it all,
My wife, my daughter, side by side, The dogs run happy, far and wide.
No need to hurry, nowhere due, Just sunlight finding pathways through,
And for a while the world can wait, Beyond the trees, beyond the gate.
Then up ahead the shadows end, The walls of green begin to bend...
And there—
Where the oaks let in the sun, Golden fields go rolling on,
Wheat beneath a boundless blue, White clouds slowly drifting through.
And I wish that time would stay, Just a little while this way,
Nothing needed, nothing done— Where the oaks let in the sun.
The pathway draws us back once more,
Beneath the green we walked before, The open sky slips out of sight,
The pathway draws us back once more, Beneath the green we walked before,
The open sky slips out of sight, Replaced by dancing shards of light.
A collar jingles somewhere near, A burst of laughter reaches here,
And leaves are stirring overhead, While sunlight dances on the path ahead.
Maybe peace is nothing more Than knowing who you're walking for.
No distant place, No grand design,
Just those I love... And borrowed time.
Where the oaks let in the sun, Golden fields go rolling on,
Wheat beneath that endless blue, And all I need is walking too.
Let the whole wide world rush by, We have leaves and fields and sky,
And nowhere else we need to run— Where the oaks let in the sun.
Then the green closes overhead, Soft leaves beneath the path we tread...
Their voices drift among the trees,
And disappear...

lines.text: Es ist die schönste Zeit des Jahres...

die Blätter hängen noch, der Sommer ist nicht weg –
doch der Handel ruft „Weihnachten“, also legt’s los.
Friede auf Erden! Zwei kaufen, drei kriegen!

Halt die Klappe und gib mir den Eierpunsch! Schon wieder Weihnachten.

ein Plastik-Rentier fast zwei Meter hoch im Raum, wir schmücken alles, als hing unser Leben dran –

Alles Gute zum Geburtstag... ...wer war das noch gleich?

Amazon klingelt, und dann schon wieder, ein Papp-Mount-Everest blockiert die Tür,
Schuldisco, Weihnachtspulli, Krippenspiel,
noch eine Mail – und dann noch eine, stündlich. Geschenke für Lehrer und Hilfskräfte,
Wichteln im Büro und drei Buffet-Termine, Mama wippt still mit ihrem Gin in der Hand,
während Papa irgendwas zusammenschraubt – und am Ende bleiben drei Schrauben übrig.

Papa flucht unterm Barbies Traumhaus,
die Anleitung ist auf Schwedisch, der Schraubenzieher krumm,
und jemand fragt, wo die letzten hundert Euro sind.
Lass es.
Einfach... lass es.

und Onkel Dave erzählt schon wieder dieselbe Story.
Die Kinder haben die Geschenke in 7,3 Sekunden zerlegt,
jetzt spielen sie den ganzen Tag mit dem Karton vom Fernseher,
